summary:
Pskov Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and the source inventory records no deviation specific to the oblast. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) contains no Northwestern Federal District findings, so the oblast is assessed against the national baseline.

That baseline is severe. Putin signed the law in 2023 prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, so legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are banned outright; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections exist. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department carries a Level 4, Do Not Travel advisory for Russia that carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Penalties are graded by role. The propaganda statute imposes administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to 4 years in prison. Under the extremism designation, participating carries 2 to 6 years and organising carries 6 to 10 years. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 convictions for extremism tied to the designated movement as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention, while 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols. Human Rights Watch states that participation in the designated organisation's activities carries up to 12 years in prison, and has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the preceding two years. The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and the Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is also documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that "Ada", a transgender woman, was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
The advisory environment for travel to Russia is unusually explicit. The US State Department's Level 4 advisory instructs citizens not to travel and names LGBT travellers as a specifically endangered category, which is a stronger signal than the underlying statutes alone convey. Human Rights Watch's June 2025 call on governments to offer safe haven to people leaving Russia treats the legal regime as a protection problem rather than a matter of individual caution.

The designation operates as a single national instrument with uneven local effects. The autonomous republic of Chechnya is named in the UK Home Office note as part of the same qualifying group, illustrating that the protection standard is applied uniformly even where conditions on the ground differ in severity between constituent territories of the Russian Federation.

Financial incentives reinforce enforcement. Meduza's reporting that propaganda-law fines yielded more than 60 million rubles for the state budget over two years indicates that the eighteenfold rise in cases is institutionally sustained rather than incidental.
localsOnly:
For residents of Pskov Oblast, the 2023 statute forecloses legal gender recognition entirely: official documents cannot be amended to reflect a person's gender, and gender-affirming surgery is prohibited. There is no administrative route by which a resident can obtain matching identification.

Russian nationals face penalties that foreigners do not, including criminal exposure. Repeat propaganda offences carry up to 4 years' imprisonment, and extremism charges carry 2 to 6 years for participation and 6 to 10 years for organising, with Human Rights Watch recording that participation in the designated organisation's activities can reach 12 years. Displaying banned symbols alone produced 98 administrative cases against 81 people between January 2024 and June 2025.

The domestic toll between 2022 and 2024 was at least 139 people affected by convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, and the death of a man held on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency, reported in December 2024, indicates the risks of pretrial detention in these cases.

Conversion-therapy confinement is documented against transgender residents: a transgender woman held for nine months near Novosibirsk from summer 2021 was forced to take testosterone and perform labour, and family members facilitated her placement. UK asylum authorities treat LGBT+ people in Russia as a particular social group for refugee purposes, which is relevant to residents considering emigration.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Pskov Oblast-specific enforcement data appears in the inventory: there are no records of arrests, raids, court outcomes or administrative cases originating in the oblast, and the 101 extremism convictions and 98 article 20.3 cases are national figures.

The sources do not establish whether Pskov Oblast has enacted local bylaws implementing the propaganda restrictions, or how oblast police and the regional prosecutor's office prioritise these offences. Local practice is not sourced either way.

Information on detention conditions within the oblast is unresolved. The inventory documents a pretrial death and police raids in Moscow, but no findings on facilities used for detainees in Pskov Oblast.

No trans-specific homicide, assault or hate-crime statistics for the oblast are available in these sources, and the inventory does not establish whether the 2023 ban displaced any gender-affirming care providers previously operating in the region.

Access to practical support within the oblast, including safe accommodation, legal assistance and any remaining community organisations, is not sourced and should be treated as unknown rather than absent.
